title: The House of the Seven Gables
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
description: The gabled house is real. It still stands on Turner Street by Salem harbour, the Turner-Ingersoll Mansion that Hawthorne knew and that is preserved today as the House of the Seven Gables museum. Around it the novel keeps its bearings in Salem: the little shop cut into the front gable, the garden and Maule's Well behind, the arched window over the by-street Hawthorne renames Pyncheon Street, and the railway on which Hepzibah and Clifford flee the town. The interiors are inferred to the real house, and Pyncheon Street is Hawthorne's name for a real Salem street, which is what the certainty labels are for.

route.displayName: The House of the Seven Gables (Turner-Ingersoll Mansion)
route.summary: The novel opens on the house itself, black in the east wind, its seven peaks pointing every way. Hawthorne makes the mansion a character before any person appears in it, carrying two centuries of Pyncheon guilt in its weather-stained timbers. The real house still stands on Turner Street.
route.note: The rusty, seven-gabled house is the real Turner-Ingersoll Mansion (1668) at 115 Derby Street on the Turner Street corner, by Salem harbour. Hawthorne knew it through his cousin Susanna Ingersoll, and it is preserved today as the House of the Seven Gables museum. The pin marks the mansion itself.

route.summary: Ruined and proud, the old gentlewoman Hepzibah must at last open a penny shop in the gable to keep from starving. She sets out gingerbread animals and marbles with a trembling hand, the final throe of what called itself old gentility. The shop is a real feature of the house, its little window still shown to visitors.
route.note: The little shop is cut into the front gable of the house, facing the street; an ancestor added the shop-door a century before. The pin sits at the Turner Street frontage of the real mansion, where such a gable shop-window would have opened.

route.summary: Phoebe finds the neglected garden behind the house, and at its centre the old spring, Maule's Well, its bewitched water shifting quaint figures over the coloured pebbles. The well carries the wizard Maule's curse into the Pyncheons' own ground; the garden and well are kept behind the real house today.
route.note: The garden and its spring lie behind the house, toward the harbour. Maule's Well is the natural spring that drew the first settler to the spot and that turned brackish after Colonel Pyncheon seized the land; the museum keeps a garden and well on the seaward side. The pin marks that ground behind the real mansion.

route.displayName: The arched window over Pyncheon Street
route.summary: Broken by thirty years' unjust imprisonment, Clifford sits at the arched window and watches the life of the street go by, a scissor-grinder, a water-cart, an organ-grinder's monkey, a passing train. The window looks out on the by-street Hawthorne renames Pyncheon Street, the real Turner Street in Salem.
route.note: Pyncheon Street is Hawthorne's name for the real by-street the house stands on, today's Turner Street in Salem. The arched window is the great second-storey window from which Clifford watches the street; the pin marks the Turner Street frontage of the house.

route.displayName: The flight by railroad from Salem
route.reference: XVII. The Flight of Two Owls
route.summary: For once seized by reckless energy, Clifford pulls Hepzibah out of the house and onto a departing train, and the two shut-in Pyncheons are swept into the great current of human life. The novel's one journey beyond the house begins at Salem's railway station.
route.note: Fleeing Judge Pyncheon's dead body in the house, Hepzibah and Clifford board a train at the town's railway station, a large structure of gray stone. Salem's depot stood off Washington Street, roughly a kilometre from the house; the pin marks that historic station area, within the book's Salem setting.
